chunks: Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Muhammad ibn al-Husayn, from Safwan, from Is'haq ibn 'Ammar, who said:

I asked Abu Ibrahim (peace be upon him) about a man who mortgages a slave, or a garment, or jewelry, or household goods. So the owner of the goods says to the mortgagee, 'You are free (permitted) to wear this garment, so wear the garment, benefit from the goods, and use the servant.' He (peace be upon him) said: 'It is permissible for him when he permits it for him, and I do not like that he does it.'

I said, 'If he mortgages a house that has a yield, for whom is the yield?' He said: 'For the owner of the house.' I said, 'If he mortgages barren land, so the owner of the land says, 'Cultivate it for yourself,' ' He said: 'This is not like that. He cultivates it for himself, and it is permissible for him just as he permitted it for him, except that he cultivates it with his own wealth and improves it.'
ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on using or benefiting from mortgaged property in Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: This hadith from al-Kafi elucidates the Shia jurisprudence of rahn (mortgage), distinguishing between movable goods and real estate by emphasizing the owner's explicit permission (ijaz) as the basis for the mortgagee's usufruct. Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) highlights the principle that while the yield of a house remains with the owner, barren land can be cultivated by the mortgagee using his own resources, reflecting the practical application of 'benefit follows the capital' in Islamic contracts. This ruling underscores the flexibility of Shia fiqh in balancing creditor rights with equitable usage of assets during the pledge period.
